# London Tenant Move-Out Checklist

A careful paper trail is the best protection when a landlord says “repairs” but the issue may be ordinary wear and tear. Use the checklist below to document the flat, the deposit position, and your position on any disputed items.

## Dispute-Proof Move-Out Records

- **Lease end date:** 2026-03-31
- **Deposit protection:** note the scheme name, deposit amount, tenancy start date, and any prescribed information you received
- **Check-in evidence:** original inventory, photos, schedule of condition, meter readings, and any email confirming the flat’s condition at move-in
- **Check-out evidence:** your own dated photos/video, keys returned, final cleaning record, and meter readings on departure
- **Repair claim details:** ask for each item claimed, the exact location, the reason it is said to be damage, the cost, and the age/expected lifespan of the item
- **Wear-and-tear context:** document length of tenancy, number of occupants, children/pets if relevant, and normal use over time
- **Communications log:** keep every message, call note, and delivery receipt in one folder

## Evidence to Gather Before You Leave

- **Photos and video**
  - Wide shots of every room
  - Close-ups of walls, floors, appliances, bathroom fittings, windows, and any pre-existing marks
  - Photos of the same areas after cleaning and just before handing back keys
  - Meter readings with the display visible
  - Photos of any items the landlord later says were damaged

- **Documents and records**
  - Tenancy agreement and any renewals
  - Inventory/check-in report
  - Deposit protection certificate and scheme details
  - Receipts for cleaning, repairs, or replacement items you paid for
  - Emails about reported defects, maintenance requests, and landlord responses
  - Proof of key return, forwarding address, and checkout appointment confirmation

- **Useful context to note**
  - Whether the item was already worn, faded, scuffed, or at end of life
  - Whether the landlord was aware of the issue during the tenancy
  - Any delay by the landlord in fixing issues you reported
  - Whether the claimed cost is for full replacement when only minor touch-up would be reasonable

## Polite Dispute Email Draft

Subject: Move-out deposit deductions and wear-and-tear items

Dear [Landlord/Agent Name],

Thank you for sending the proposed deductions from my deposit for the flat at [address].

I do not agree that the items listed should be treated as tenant damage where they appear to be consistent with fair wear and tear, age, or pre-existing condition. As the tenancy ends on 2026-03-31, I would be grateful if you could provide:

- the check-in and check-out inventories
- dated photos supporting each claimed item
- an explanation of why each item is said to be beyond normal wear and tear
- the repair or replacement invoice or estimate for each item
- the age of the item and any allowance for depreciation

For my part, I have kept records of the condition of the property, cleaning, meter readings, and key return. I am happy to review any specific item in detail and to resolve this amicably.

Please treat this email as a request to discuss the deductions without admission of liability. I reserve all rights in relation to the deposit.

Kind regards,
[Your name]
[Forwarding address]
[Phone number]

## Wording to Avoid Admitting Liability

Use neutral language. Avoid phrases like:
- “Sorry, I damaged it”
- “I’ll pay for the repairs”
- “It was my fault”
- “I should have looked after it better”
- “Please take it from my deposit”
- “I admit responsibility”
- “I agree the damage was caused by me”

Safer alternatives:
- “I do not accept that this item is tenant damage.”
- “This appears consistent with normal wear and tear.”
- “I would like to see the supporting evidence for the deduction.”
- “I do not admit liability.”
- “Please provide the basis for the amount claimed.”

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Dispute a deduction] https://www.gov.uk/tenancy-deposit-protection/if-your-landlord-doesnt-protect-your-deposit
Action: [Button: Letter template] https://england.shelter.org.uk/housing_advice/tenancy_deposits

## Sources

- UK deposit protection overview: https://www.gov.uk/tenancy-deposit-protection
- Shelter tenancy deposit advice: https://england.shelter.org.uk/housing_advice/tenancy_deposits
- Citizens Advice on tenancy deposits: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/housing/renting-a-home/tenancy-deposits/
